utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender from both parties? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The witnesses that we had mentioned briefly before that we had attached to our materials regarding 92 bis, that would be PS1 - that was Witness I;- PS2; Mrs. Ibrahimefendic; PS3, which was Witness DD; PS4, Witness L. And I'm told PS3 should be under seal. Also, Mr. President, the -- and I apologise for not dealing with this earlier, but I now understand from the Court's ruling that I should offer into evidence the attachment, the information report that I attached on our supplemental filing relating to Mr. Nikolic's responses to the two issues that were brought up there, Mr. -- regarding Mr. Franken's testimony and -- and the issue related to the boundaries of -- of the Bratunac Brigade. That was not meant to be used against Mr. Nikolic in any way but just to help assist the Court on these issues of cooperation and credibility. Also, as the Court is aware, this -- in reviewing cooperation, the testimony of Mr. Nikolic at the trial of Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic was fundamental to this agreement, and I would offer at this time that testimony into the record. I -- that -- I'm sorry, I failed to offer that earlier. It just didn't cross my mind, it was so fundamental. But I should have, and I do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. Nikolic's Defence counsel has no objections to the proposals made by my learned colleague from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As for the documents PS1 to PS4, I believe during our Status Conference of this case this Trial Chamber has already made a ruling that they admitted into evidence. Well, at this moment, I would like to reiterate our decision made at that time. And frankly speaking, I don't know whether during the pre-trial stage, especially during the Status Conference, whether we could admit anything to the evidence or not. But anyway, they are admitted into evidence. As for the testimony of Mr. Nikolic during another case, I believe that the testimony is relevant to this proceedings and not only in the testimony of -- the testimony not only in the direct examination but also in the cross- examination admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. As for the information report mentioned by the Prosecution, we have some doubts about it because those corrections were concerning with the testimony in other case, and it is a report that was conducted only between Mr. Nikolic and the Prosecution. So in accordance with the usual practice, this report is not admitted into the evidence in this case. But if Mr. Nikolic wants to make some clarifications or wants to make some comments on those information report, please feel free to do so at a later stage. Do you understand, Mr. Nikolic? Thank you. Thank you very --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours. I understand what you have said. And for the sake of the truth, with regard to those two issues, I think it would be useful if you allowed me to address you and to provide certain clarifications that I think might be quite important and which will enable you to assess this matter. I think that I could provide you with clarifications with regard to both issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I hope you could do that at a later stage, because we'll give you an opportunity to make a statement after the closing arguments by your counsel. Is that agreeable to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours. Whenever you decide, I will be prepared to provide further clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any closing argument? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just have a few words to say. And as you know, since we're here pursuant to a plea agreement and pursuant to Mr. Nikolic's plea, I think this Court knows, as does anyone involved in a criminal justice system, that the victims can never truly find satisfaction or -- or what they need. There's no way that I can speak to the Srebrenica women and tell them that -- that I can give them anything but some justice, some hope that things will be better. Of course, this was true in any system, whether it be a rape victim, a robbery victim, or a murder victim. But having said that, I think that there are positive things that come out of such a plea and such an agreement, and that is why I think the Prosecution's recommendation of 15 to 20 years is fair and just. And I'll just take a few moments this afternoon to explain to you why I think that's true. I don't think the Defence's recommendation is fair or just. First of all, in looking at the -- the bigger picture, I think we know we're not just a domestic court. We -- we're here to not only bring justice to wherever we can for the former Yugoslavia but also reconciliation is important. And I think the broader history of the area and the people look to us in some way for reconciliation as well as justice. And so if I look at the big picture: We have Mr. Nikolic, the first VRS officer to stand up and take responsibility for what was the worst massacre in this war. Now, taking responsibility is a very important step towards reconciliation. Now, I'm not naive. I know that responsibility had something to do with SFOR and the amount of evidence in this case. But given that, setting that aside, it was not an easy thing to do, and he's stood in front of this Court and testified at length and told you what he did and what happened around him, and that is something of great significance. And I think it's of significance for a couple of reasons: One, as the first officer to stand up and say this happened, followed shortly by Dragan Obrenovic, Mr. Nikolic has let the -- the world know and especially those Muslims know that yes, it did happen; I as a Serb and I as a man are not afraid to tell that and admit it happened. And I know, and I think the Court knows now, or will know as they review the documents that the Defence will also talk about, that this has a very important and significant meaning to many Muslims. We've seen the article of Emir Suljagic, a victim of Srebrenica, and how much that meant to him, how he described the great relief he felt for the first time since -- since Potocari. This relief, I can't put a value on that relief, the relief of one Muslim man. That is a great value. That is of great significance. And he is certainly not the only one that has felt that. Many, many Muslims have felt that. And I give some credit to Mr. Nikolic for being able to start that and bring those feelings throughout Bosnia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Also, bringing this truth to light in such a stark and definitive and final way places the Republika Srpska, the government that has, as you know, denied that this has happened and has suggested the Muslims have killed themselves, it now puts them in a situation where they must either face the truth and acknowledge it, which would be a huge step towards reconciliation and a major historical move. Now, I'm not so naive as that because of Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic that the RS will make that move. I hope they will. But if they don't, they are now putting themselves aside the world community, where the truth is out, the admissions are made, the record is clear, and they must have to face that and go on in a government like that. So that is of some value. I'd gives them the ability to face the truth and join the world community or continue to follow the lie and push themselves aside. And it was Mr. Nikolic, followed by Mr. Obrenovic, that have set this historical movement in motion. Now, that -- that is the bigger picture, and I think the letter of Abdurahman Malkic and others will help fill in the blanks, and I'm sure Mr. Londrovic will very eloquently discuss that. But now getting back -- let's get down to our picture here in The Hague. Of what value is this? Well, Mr. Nikolic has provided us with an insider's account of what happened. And after seven years of investigation and hearing one -- fundamentally one VRS soldier, Drazan Erdemovic, be able to provide an account of a major execution, this is the first time that we really see in a large scale an officer able to explain the big picture. And there -- this is will be something. This is a record that you as the Judges will have to judge this case will always be able to go back to, to compare the other witnesses, to see what other witnesses say. Now, it will be your decision how much credibility to give Mr. Nikolic, of course, but you're able to see him testify; you were able to see his tone, his voice; you were able to see how he reacted under very difficult cross- examination. So you're the best -- in the best position to judge his credibility, and that record that he has given you is an incredibly valuable insight from the inside, something that is -- is rare, certainly in this Tribunal, and even in other criminal cases. And it has value, especially has value not just on its own merits as you view it and how -- the reliability you give it, but you will be able to compare it to the record: the Muslims that have testified, the Muslims that have -- are in the record for 92 bis, the DutchBat soldiers, the Serb soldiers. You will be able to view his credibility in relation to what you feel has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt so you can judge his credibility. This is an invaluable thing for you to have in order to make this very difficult judgement, as any judgement would be, and I -- and it's something that is -- is of great importance, especially Potocari. Potocari, the days of Potocari, the numbers of witnesses, the confusion there, the -- the abuses, the separations, this -- as this was presented in the Krstic case and in full is a massive undertaking, and to understand it all is not difficult but it is a -- it's a huge task. This task of understanding Potocari, what happened there, the units that were involved, is made so much clearer by Mr. Nikolic's testimony because we know what happened. We know from the Muslims, from the Dutch -- fundamentally we know many of the people that did it. But now you see it from his perspective, and it really binds the whole story. So we now know from Potocari, without a shadow of a doubt, what happened there. This is very valuable. Without that testimony, yes, you would have known and you would have sorted it out - no question about it - but this is clearly a valuable testimony. Another factor I think you should consider is, as I mentioned briefly in our papers, there are many Muslims that the Prosecution has not had to call because Mr. Nikolic has pled guilty. Some we've been able to put in through 92 bis, many; and others I've not had to call at all. And this is a tremendous relief for those people that have come up here once before, many of them, and for some that haven't come up. There was a witness that I -- we were going to have to arrest to bring her here because her testimony was so important. We didn't have to do that, thank goodness. I'm not sure I would have, but -- the anguish and the difficulty of going through this process was set aside for many, many victims and witnesses. There should be future Srebrenica cases, and by this agreement Mr. Nikolic has agreed to testify in each of those, and that will be of course of great value, as it was in this case. And I have no doubt that he will follow through on his commitment, even after sentencing, and that is of tremendous value for the Office of the Prosecutor for all the reasons I've already mentioned. And lastly, as Your Honours know, Mr. Nikolic has in addition to agreeing to cooperate for all the Srebrenica cases of 1995 - that was part of the plea agreement - in addition to that plea agreement, he has offered his cooperation for the entire wartime period and without reservation. And now, that process has not had a chance to really go forward. I can't offer you the -- the ultimate value of that at this point, but it is valuable for the same reasons that it was valuable in this case. So those are the fundamental reasons why I think this is a fair and just sentence range, and I sincerely ask Your Honours to take these remarks into consideration in your review of sentence, because it's very important. This process that we've entered into is very important. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the accused, Mr. Momir Nikolic, a Serb from Bosnia and Herzegovina, is here before you. He was arrested in his home in Bratunac on the 1st of April, 2002 and he was transferred to the Detention Unit, the UN Detention Unit in Scheveningen, on the 2nd of April, 2002. You have to decide on the appropriate sentence for him because on the 7th of May, 2003 he entered a guilty plea on Count 5 in the amended and separated indictment. He pleaded guilty to the crime of persecution, punishable under Article 5(H) of the Tribunal's Statute. According to applicable law when determining the sentence, that is, according to Article 24 of the Statute and Rule 101 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Defence counsel of Mr. Nikolic would not want to discuss Momir Nikolic's sentence at the time because we are convinced that the Trial Chamber is fully aware of these facts, of these matters. But the Defence will try not to repeat itself, because according to the law on meting out sentencing, it has fully expanded its views on this in its sentencing brief, which it submitted to the Trial Chamber on the 14th of July, 2003. The Defence would like to draw attention to certain facts that in our opinion should be taken into consideration when determining the sentence and which in practice to date, before these -- this Tribunal have not been taken into consideration. The practice concerning sentences in courts of Yugoslavia, the gravity of the crime, the degree to which the accused participant -- the accused participated in the crime, and all mitigating and aggravating factors should be taken into consideration. Article 21, item 1 of the Statute of the Tribunal and 101(B)(iii) (e) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require the Tribunal to take into consideration the general practice in sentencing in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. The practice of this Tribunal to date has shown that Trial Chambers are not bound to adhere to these principles, and Mr. Momir Nikolic's Defence counsel agrees with this, but we believe that Trial Chambers should refer to these principles because that would assist the Trial Chambers to determine the appropriate sentence. Mr. Nikolic's Defence counsel agrees that the gravity of the crime is the primary factor that should be taken into consideration when determining the sentence. The sentence meted out should reflect the gravity of the accused's crime. Determining the gravity of the crime involves taking into consideration all the details and circumstances of the case and the degree to which the accused participated in the criminal offence. Similarly, our view is that the sentence has to reflect the importance and the role that the accused play within the context of the conflict in the former Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslavia. This is a view that has been expressed in Tuta, Naletilic and Martinovic case, the judgement dated the 31st of March, 2002, paragraph 744. The Defence counsel accepts the finding that the massacre that followed after the Serbs had taken over Srebrenica is one of the worst crimes in Europe after the Second World War, since the Second World War. However, although this is not in dispute, this should not obscure the fact that the main factor is the individual responsibility -- is individual responsibility, the principle of individual responsibility before this Tribunal. The gravity of the crime and the degree to which Momir Nikolic participated in that crime has been described in detail, under item 5 of the amended indictment and in the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, and the Defence does not want to go over them once again. But in order to assist the Trial Chamber when determining the gravity of the crime, the form and degree to which Momir Nikolic participated in that crime, with all due respect, the Defence claims that the Trial Chamber must take into consideration the fact that Momir Nikolic's role was not of crucial significance when compared to the role played by other co-perpetrators. The Defence of Mr. Nikolic wishes to point out that the events in Srebrenica in July of 1995, although extremely large in scope, have to be distinguished from the overall systematic campaign of forcible ethnic separation and ethnic cleansing, which was planned, thought up, and implemented by a large number of individuals in the Bosnian Serb leadership, the leaders of the SDS and the government of Republika Srpska, including Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Ratko Mladic. It is also the view of the Defence that the forcible removal of the population and the murders of the fall of the Srebrenica enclave could only take place because of the atmosphere of hatred between the Bosnian Serbs and the non-Serb population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was initiated by the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, the leadership of the SDS, and the government of the Republika Srpska. Mr. Nikolic, who was a teacher by profession, and was not an active member of the military, was mobilised in April 1992. He was not involved in the planning of the forcible expulsion. Mr. Nikolic was not in a position of command responsibility and only performed tasks passed on to him by superior officers. Since all plans and decisions regarding the forcible transfer and the subsequent murder operation were either made by the Main Staff of the VRS or the VRS Drina Corps command, including security and intelligence officers without any personal involvement by Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Nikolic's main participation was in helping to coordinate and organise the transportation of the women and children to Kladanj, the separation and detention of able-bodied Muslim men, in conjunction with other VRS and MUP units. Although Mr. Nikolic was personally aware of many Muslim men being abused and assaulted and did nothing to prevent these abuses, he was never personally engaged in such conduct, nor did he ever take any part in executions. The Defence of Mr. Nikolic wishes to compare Mr. Nikolic's case to the case of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. Your Honours must be aware that both Mr. Nikolic and Mrs. Plavsic pleaded guilty for persecution, a crime against humanity, before the start of their trials. The persecution campaign in the Plavsic case included the persecution of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and other non-Serbs in 37 municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The persecution campaign in the Nikolic case relates only to the Muslims of Srebrenica and to only one municipality, the Srebrenica municipality. In the persecution campaign in the Plavsic case, at least 50.000 persons were killed, while in the campaign in the Nikolic case around 7.000 persons were killed. In the Plavsic case, the persecution campaign lasted longer, from the 1st of July, 1991 to the 30th of December, 1992, while in the Nikolic case it lasted from the 4th of July, 1995 to the 1st of November, 1995. Biljana Plavsic bears both individual and command responsibility,0002 while Momir Nikolic bears only individual responsibility. He is not charged with command responsibility in the indictment, under Article 7(3) of the Tribunal. Biljana Plavsic did not testify; she did not cooperate with the Office of the Prosecutor, and Momir Nikolic did and will continue to cooperate with the Office of the Prosecutor. Momir Nikolic has shown substantial cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor, which was not done by Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. Mrs. Biljana Plavsic was one of the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, while nothing like that can be said about Mr. Momir Nikolic. Momir Nikolic was the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the Bratunac Brigade. He was not an authorised official with an official pass, and he did not even have the capacity to instigate criminal proceedings for crimes committed. Your Honours are aware of the fact that Mrs. Plavsic was sentenced to 11 years of imprisonment. The Office of the Prosecutor proposed that she be sentenced to 15 to 25 years. This sentence became valid, and now Mrs. Plavsic is serving her sentence in Sweden. Bearing all this in mind, the Defence of Mr. Nikolic, with all due respect, argues that it would not be fitting for Momir Nikolic to be sentenced to a longer period of time than Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. With respect to aggravating circumstances, the Defence of Mr. Nikolic argues that there is no aggravating circumstance in the case of Momir Nikolic. In contrast to the Defence, the Prosecution points out that in Momir Nikolic's case there are three such circumstances, these being his position of leadership, the vulnerability of the victims, and0003 the depravity of the crimes. With respect to his position of leadership, the Prosecutor points out that Mr. Nikolic was a commander in organising activities and managing the activities of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. The Defence disagrees with this viewpoint of the Prosecution and stresses that Momir Nikolic, as the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the Bratunac Infantry Brigade, was duty-bound to, in connection with the commanding officer of the unit within which his unit was, to suggest the use of the military police. He was responsible for the combat readiness of the military police and for the implementation of the military police tasks. But it was the commanding officer of the military unit that commanded this unit or the commanding officer of the institution of which the military police formed a part. In this particular case, this would be the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. The accused, Mr. Nikolic, did not have command responsibility, nor was he charged with command responsibility in the indictment. The Prosecutor gives certain examples: Dario Kordic was the leader of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and his position can be equated with the position taken by Mr. Radovan Karadzic in Republika Srpska and by no means with the position of Momir Nikolic. Jean Kambanda, as the Prosecution points out themselves, held a high-ranking ministerial position, which is certainly not the case with Momir Nikolic. Mario Cerkez was a brigade commander; this position cannot be equated with Momir Nikolic's position either. Kupreskic was the commander of a battalion of the military police, and again this cannot be equated with0004 Momir Nikolic's position. All the accused that the Prosecutor refers to had command responsibility in addition to individual responsibility. This is not the case with Mr. Nikolic. The Prosecution further points out that Mr. Nikolic played an important role in the forcible transfer of the civilian population, the separation, detention, and abuse of men separated off in Potocari and arrested on the Bratunac-Milici road. The Prosecution further points out that Mr. Nikolic was responsible for the coordination of these activities with his superior officers. The Defence does not challenge any of these facts, and Mr. Nikolic has admitted them. But they are listed in the indictment against Mr. Nikolic, and Mr. Nikolic's Defence contends that Mr. Nikolic had he not done these things would not have been indicted. All this is in the indictment against Mr. Nikolic and all this is subsumed in the overall Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. gravity of the offence, so the Defence, with all due respect, argues that it cannot be taken as a special aggravating circumstance. With respect to the vulnerability of the victims and the depravity of the crime, the Defence agrees that these can be aggravating circumstances but the Defence contends that in all the circumstances of this case these factors are, in fact, subsumed in the overall gravity of the offence, and with all due respect, we suggest to the Trial Chamber that they should not be viewed as special aggravating circumstances, and this was the manner in which the Trial Chamber proceeded in the case of Mrs. Plavsic, the sentence of the 27th of February, 2003, paragraph 78. In the case of Momir Nikolic, there are a number of mitigating circumstances which form a substantial body of mitigation and lead us to argue that he should be entitled to a reduced sentence. One of these substantial mitigating circumstances is his guilty plea. In the practice of the Tribunal, a guilty plea is a reason to diminish the sentence to which the accused would otherwise be sentenced for the following reasons: A guilty plea demonstrates honesty and is very important for the Tribunal because it encourages others to come forth, regardless of whether they are already indicted or are unknown perpetrators; a guilty plea contributes to the fundamental mission of the Tribunal, to establish the truth in connection with the crimes over which it has jurisdiction; a guilty plea provides a unique and unquestionable fact-finding tool that greatly contributes to peace-building and reconciliation among the affected communities. That this is so is best illustrated by the testimonies of DA and DB, Defence witnesses, as well as the Defence exhibits marked DS17, DS18, and DS19. A guilty plea contributes to the public advantage of the work of the International Tribunal by saving significant resources for investigations, fees for Defence counsel, and the costs of a trial; a guilty plea also may relieve some victims and witnesses from the stress of giving evidence. Mr. Nikolic's plea demonstrates his honesty and candour. His plea deserves special attention since he was the first Serbian officer to come forth and to acknowledge the VRS's involvement and his personal responsibility with regard to the events of the fall of the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995. His acknowledgment of the crimes and his personal accountability will contribute to rendering justice to victims, to deterring others, to providing a basis for reconciliation, and to preclude ethnic hatred. This leads us to the core mission of this Tribunal, to restore peace and security to the region through accountability and reconciliation. In view of the fact that Mr. Nikolic pleaded guilty before the start of the trial, the Defence asserts that he deserves full credit for his guilty plea. The second important mitigating circumstance in favour of Mr. Nikolic is his substantial cooperation, which he has already realised with the Office of the Prosecutor. Rule 101(B)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence explicitly states that cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor should be considered in sentencing an accused who has been found guilty. Moreover, cooperation with the Prosecutor is the only circumstance explicitly provided for within the terms of the Rules. By this simple fact, it takes on a special importance. The Defence argues that in this case there has been substantial cooperation between Mr. Nikolic and the Prosecution and the Prosecution itself has confirmed this in their additional written submission or, rather, in their additional sentencing brief of the 15th of October, 2003. The statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility is a good example of high-quality information given to the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Nikolic has given names, described incidents, explained the participation of military and police units, and provided other information not previously available to the Office of the Prosecutor before Mr. Nikolic gave extensive interviews to the Office of the Prosecutor. The Defence, with all due respect, wishes to point out to the Trial Chamber that it should also take into consideration the fact that Mr. Nikolic's decision to cooperate with the Office of the Prosecutor as the first Serbian officer to do so required special courage, in view to have fact that even the official authorities of Republika Srpska have not yet admitted the crimes that took place after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. We argue that the cooperation of Mr. Nikolic with the Prosecutor has obviously encouraged and will encourage others to come forward and to accept their responsibility. Their Honours certainly know that after Mr. Nikolic's guilty plea, Mr. Dragan Obrenovic also pleaded guilty and decided to cooperate with the Office of the Prosecutor, and this was followed by other guilty pleas; Mr. Nikolic has certainly contributed to this, at least in part. The third important mitigating circumstance is his remorse, which is sincere. Sincere remorse has been taken as a mitigating factor in a number of cases before the Tribunal. In the Simic case, paragraph 92 of the sentence; the Sikirica and others case, sentence, paragraph 192, 194, and 230; the Todorovic case, paragraph 89 of the sentencing brief; Plavsic case, sentencing judgement, paragraph 73. Mr. Nikolic has accepted responsibility and shown sincere remorse during his meeting with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. By his guilty plea, Mr. Nikolic has also demonstrated remorse publicly. Mr. Nikolic intends to address the Trial Chamber to repeat his expression of sincere remorse, and the Defence hopes that the Trial Chamber will grant him leave to do so. The fact that Mr. Nikolic had no opportunity for voluntary surrender to the Tribunal, in the Tribunal jurisprudence voluntary surrender has been taken as a mitigating factor. In the Simic case, sentencing judgement paragraph 107; in the Kunarac case, sentencing judgement paragraph 168. Mr. Nikolic did not voluntarily surrender because he did not know of the sealed indictment, and he did not know that the indictment against him had been confirmed on the 28th of March, 2002, only a few days before his arrest, that is, the 1st of April, 2002. Mr. Nikolic, therefore, did not have an opportunity for voluntary surrender. The Trial Chamber, in the view of the Defence, should take into consideration as an equally mitigating circumstance the cooperation of Mr. Nikolic and his correct behaviour toward the investigators of the Tribunal before his arrest, which is proved by Mr. Ken Corlett's statement of the 17th of June, 2003, Defence Exhibit DS1. Mr. Nikolic responded to all requests by the Tribunal investigators. He did not change his place of residence, nor did he try to hide in any other way. He was arrested at the address he had always resided at, which was well known to Tribunal investigators. The Defence of Mr. Nikolic, with all due respect, contends that Mr. Nikolic -- had he known that a secret indictment had been issued against him, had he had someone to tell him this, as Mrs. Plavsic did -- he would certainly have voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal. And this is confirmed by Witness Milorad Krsmanovic. Another mitigating circumstance, which in the view of the Defence Mr. Nikolic has a right to, is no prior criminal convictions. In the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal, a lack of prior criminal record has been considered as a mitigating factor: Simic case, sentencing judgement, paragraph 108; Aleksovski case, sentencing judgement, paragraph 236. Therefore, the Trial Chamber, when determining a sentence, should take into consideration the fact that Mr. Nikolic had no previous convictions and consider this a mitigating circumstance; the Defence Exhibits DS2 and DS3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Londrovic, it's time for a break. Shall we break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have just finished the part that concerns mitigating circumstances, and I was going on to the following item. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll break until 4.00 -- 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Londrovic. Please proceed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The fact that there's been no prior discriminatory behaviour, in the Defence's opinion, is also a factor that the Trial Chamber should take into consideration as a mitigating circumstance. Momir Nikolic was born in Bratunac on the 20th of February, 1955. After attending the primary school and secondary school in Bratunac, he graduated from the university in Sarajevo and started working as a professor -- as a teacher in the secondary school in Bratunac. He married, and he has two sons. His elder son, Branislav, is studying in Belgrade, and his younger son, Aleksandar, attends primary school in Bratunac. The Defence would like to stress the fact that up until the time when he committed the crime, Mr. Nikolic led an honest, private family and social life. He never showed any nationalistic tendencies and never had any problems with members of other ethnic groups. Mr. Nikolic did not discriminate against his pupils on an ethnic basis, and he socialised with people from various ethnic groups. At a time of growing inter-ethnic tension in Bosnia-Herzegovina, between 1989 and 1991, Momir Nikolic did not support the idea of a Greater Serbia, and he was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. Likewise, he did not participate in any of the numerous nationalistic rallies which at the time had been organised by the nationalistic parties. All this has been proven by statements from Defence witnesses and by the exhibits that have been presented to the Trial Chamber. After the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement, Mr. Nikolic was demobilised. He left the Republika Srpska army and had various jobs in Bratunac, which is something he's already mentioned in his testimony. During that period, he cared not only for his two sons and his wife but also for his 70-year-old mother, Milenija Nikolic, who lives with his family. From the time of his arrest, Mr. Nikolic's family has had to cover all the costs of living out of Mr. Nikolic's wife's salary as a teacher, which amounts to 428 convertible marks a month, and from his mother's pension, which is 79.90 convertible marks a month. The financial and economic situation of Mr. Nikolic's family is thus quite difficult, and in the Defence's opinion, the Trial Chamber should also take this factor into consideration as a mitigating circumstance for Mr. Nikolic. Another mitigating circumstance in favour of Mr. Nikolic is his conduct in the UN Detention Unit. During his stay in the Detention Unit, Mr. Nikolic has fully respected the prescribed rules and conditions of detention, and he has behaved towards the staff of the Detention Unit in an exemplary fashion. And he behaved in the same manner towards all the other accused, regardless of the ethnic group they belonged to. This can be proven by a statement from -- by a report from the UN Detention Unit; this is Defence Exhibit DS14. As far as the witness Milivoje Petkovic's testimony is concerned and the protected witness who testified in closed session, with regard to this testimony, once the testimony is analysed, the Trial Chamber can draw the conclusion that, on the whole, these testimonies confirm the event that Mr. Nikolic spoke about for the first time when he testified. It would not be reasonable to expect that Mr. Mile Petrovic would admit that he participated in the elimination of captured Muslims, because if he did this, he would expose himself to criminal responsibility. As far as the credibility of Mr. Momir Nikolic as a witness is concerned and as far as his truthful and courageous testimony is concerned, the Defence would like to point out that with regard to this matter, it fully agrees with the positions of the Defence which are provided -- which are listed in their additional sentencing brief, provided to the Trial Chamber on the 15th of October, 2003. The significance for the Bosniak people of the admission of guilt and the acceptance of responsibility on the part of Mr. Nikolic can be best seen from the letter of the current major of Srebrenica, Mr. Malkic, Defence Exhibit DS17. In this letter, it says: "Momir Nikolic is the first officer of the Serbian army who found the courage and strength to admit the crimes and the fact that he participated in these crimes himself. I hope that his conscience has been awoken and this is why I support his guilty plea, his admission of guilt, and I appeal to others to do the same. The admission of the crime committed against the residents of Srebrenica is of multi-fold importance, when we know that Republika Srpska authorities have not officially admitted it yet. I believe that not only Momir Nikolic and others confessing their personal responsibility, but the clarification of the role of others in the Serbian army and officials of the Serbian people will force the Republika Srpska authorities to finally admit that a crime was perpetrated in Srebrenica by individuals and groups from the ranks of the Serbian people. It is only by recognising and admitting the real and whole truth about the crime committed in July 1995 and other crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is only through this means that trust can be rebuilt among the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina." On the basis of everything that has been set forth, Mr. Nikolic's Defence counsel, with all due respect, requests that the Trial Chamber not determine a sentence exceeding ten years and that this sentence should take into account the time that Momir Nikolic has already spent in the Detention Unit. I would now like to require that the Trial Chamber grant Mr. Nikolic permission to address you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Londrovic. And before we give the floor to Mr. Nikolic, I would like to ask you two questions: In your sentencing brief, you indicated in paragraph 16 that "Following the abolishment of the death penalty, the maximum sentence is 20 years." But it appears that Article 38 of the Bosnia code states "20 to 40 years." Would you please make some clarifications on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I can provide you with some clarifications. Before the war broke out and before the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia disintegrated, according to the former legislation of the former Yugoslavia and the former republics within Yugoslavia, the maximum sentence for the most serious crimes was the death penalty, whereas the maximum term of imprisonment was 15 years. The courts in the former Yugoslavia, in the case of the most serious crimes, if they had determined that there were reasons not to issue the death penalty, they could replace the death penalty by a sentence of 20 years in prison. It follows that in the courts of the former Yugoslavia the maximum sentence was 15 years in prison or, rather, the death penalty could be replaced by a sentence of 20 years in prison. It was not possible to determine a sentence within a 15-to-20-year range. You couldn't give a sentence of 16, 17, or 18 years. The maximum sentence was 15 years, or if the court decided not to opt for the death penalty, then that penalty would be replaced by a 20-year sentence. The criminal law in Yugoslavia was subsequently amended; the death penalty was abolished. So the possibility remained of meting out a 15-year prison sentence for serious crimes. Or if the penalty was to replace the death penalty, the term of imprisonment would be 20 years. You mentioned an article from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This law was adopted in 1988. And when the criminal law of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina abolished the death penalty, then the sentence of long-term imprisonment was introduced, which could range from 20 to 40 years. However, since Mr. Nikolic committed a crime in 1995, and according to the criminal legislation of Yugoslavia, one always opts for the more lenient sentence. For this reason, we claim that for the crime that Mr. Nikolic is being charged with, according to the law in the former Yugoslavia, the maximum sentence would be 20 years in prison, if the death penalty were to be replaced with a 20-year prison sentence and if the death penalty were abolished. According to the Tribunal's positions, according to the Tribunal's jurisprudence, life imprisonment would more or less be equivalent to the death penalty that had been provided for by the legislation in the former Yugoslavia, the former legislation in the former Yugoslavia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honour, we have to distinguish between the criminal law of the Bosnia- Herzegovina Federation, which is one entity, and the criminal law of Republika Srpska, which has its own criminal law and is a separate entity. And you are well aware that Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of these two entities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware that this Tribunal will not bound by the national practice in meting out this sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I am aware of that fact. And in my closing argument, I did stress that fact. I pointed out that according to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, this Tribunal is not bound by the general practice of sentencing in the former Yugoslavia. And I stated that Mr. Nikolic's Defence accepted this. However, we have appealed to you to bear these principles in mind, as they might assist you to determine the appropriate sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and the position of this Tribunal. Do you have an opportunity to explain to your client about the seriousness of the crime of persecution as a crime against humanity and the sentencing range for that crime in this Tribunal, which I believe is from more or less seven years to the life sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My colleague Kirsch and I fully explained the gravity of the crime that he has admitted. The accused is aware of the seriousness of the crime. And when he entered a guilty plea, you may recall that this Trial Chamber drew his attention to the fact that they weren't bound by agreements, and Mr. Nikolic told you that he was aware of that fact and that he was aware of the fact that for the crime of persecution, which is punishable under Article 5(H) of the Statute, he stated that he was aware of the fact that he could be given a sentence of life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, well, you may sit down while making your statement. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, if I have understood the authorisation you granted a little earlier on, I've been granted leave to clarify two issues; the first one concerns my request relating to certain funds of the officer from the Dutch Battalion, and the second issue has to do with the zone of responsibility or, rather, has to do with Kravica and with my view of the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. I would first of all like to try and explain this matter to you, the matter that has to do with the statement given by the officer from the Dutch Battalion. In response to a question put to me by Mr. Karnavas, I was a little confused by his question when it was stated that I asked from the Dutch Battalion officer, I asked for remuneration for his rent. That concerned the Dutch Battalion. At that time, I said - and I will repeat this again - that the Dutch Battalion was only billeted in the UN headquarters in Potocari. At the time, I didn't pay attention to the fact that during that period in Bratunac military observers were in the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac, UN military observers. They stayed there together with their interpreters. They paid for their accommodation and for their food in the hotel in Bratunac. As far as the observers are concerned, they paid for their accommodation to Hotel Fontana, or, rather, to the Podrinje company, and they would pay for their accommodation when they got funds from their base or from their command in Tuzla. When the attack was launched against Srebrenica, a group of these military observers withdrew to their base in Potocari and to Srebrenica, and it is possible that during that period they had failed to pay that company, that is to say, they failed to pay for their accommodation in the Fontana Hotel, which is where they had been staying. What is my connection with this matter? I will tell you about it very briefly now. Before me I have some documents on the basis of which the Trial Chamber can see that by an order from the corps commander, General Zivanovic, I was designated as the controlling organ for all the payments made to that company, all the trade to that company, and that concerned all transactions with the Dutch Battalion and all the organisations which traded with the Podrinje company from Bratunac, that is to say, with the hotel in Bratunac. I have an order here before me which I can provide you with. It is dated the 10th of August, 1994, number 402-2. It's signed by Major Milenko Zivanovic, and it is signed and sealed and stamped. In the penultimate paragraph, you can see that I represent the security organ from the Bratunac Brigade and that these duties are my responsibility. I am supposed to control these transactions. The following document that I can show you is another order issued by General Zivanovic, the corps commander, and that document demonstrates - and I quote - "The entire procedure that has to do with providing UNPROFOR members with goods, members who were located in Srebrenica. And the commander of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade shall control all these deliveries, all these procedures." And, Your Honour, what does that have to do with the Bratunac Brigade? What do financial transactions have to do with the Bratunac Brigade? Well, I have a document here from that company, from the Podrinje company in Bratunac, and this document shows that a letter addressed to the general or the corps command -- well, I will quote: "You are aware that we provide logistical support for these transactions for the Bratunac Brigade and there will be a 70-per cent benefit and it is planned that 300.000 dinars should be separated by the end of the year for the brigade." For all of these reasons, my role was to control the trade and to control all the documents that formed part of the financial transactions of that company. And before this Trial Chamber, I would like to state that it is possible that at the time when I had contact, when I contacted the representative of the Dutch Battalion, I requested that the debts be paid, the debts for staying in the Hotel Fontana and for being -- and for food consumed in the Hotel Fontana. But I would like to claim that I never asked anyone -- I never asked any Dutch Battalion members for funds for my personal use. Only what I have mentioned is possible, because these documents that I have before me provide proof -- these documents have been stamped, and they prove that the Dutch would pay in cash and that the military observers would pay in the way that I have explained to you. Your Honours, I wish to show you or tender into evidence all these documents that I have, and all of these have to do with trade payments and all the circumstances that have to do with the military observers, the Hotel Fontana, that is, the Podrinje company, and the Dutch Battalion, Hotel Fontana, and the Podrinje company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the tendering of those documents into the evidence, I believe that we could find another opportunity in other proceedings. Do you have any observations to make, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Observations to do with this issue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It may -- well, it depends. If you have some issues to deal with on this issue, you may continue. And if not -- if you have any other observations, you may make it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to ask you, if you have any questions to ask in connection with what I have just said, please do so. And then I would like to say something about another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me there's no questions to ask you on this issue from the Bench. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another issue I wanted to tell you the full truth about was the issue of the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. In my testimony, I said that I am not an expert on such questions and that these fall within the competence of the operative organs, the chief of staff, and the brigade commander. I did not wish then, nor do I wish now, to go into an expert analysis of the area of responsibility, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because I feel I am not fully familiar with these questions. What I can say now is that after my testimony I looked at the brigade rules and then I was in a dilemma as to its position: Was it a brigade in defence, which it certainly cannot be? Was it a brigade on the offensive? And again, I cannot describe it as such, because it wasn't. But thinking about its position, I thought that it was on the defence, because it wasn't moving anywhere. The units were simply holding their positions. And now I know that any unit, even a low-level unit - and this includes a brigade - has its area of responsibility in depth. And, of course, if that is the case, the Bratunac Brigade, in view of the fact that it also had a battalion attached to it, so its area of responsibility was extended -- in view of this fact, I can now say that Kravica was within the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. This was what I wanted to add, but I certainly don't want to --to assume the right of commenting on this area, because as an intelligence officer I was interested in what was in front of the Bratunac Brigade units and that was what was in the enclave or, if we are speaking of combat, what was in the direction of the operations carried out by the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Nikolic, if you have -- if you have any other observations to make.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished with this issue. If Your Honours have any question about this issue, I am prepared to reply to the extent to which I understand these matters. Then I would like to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may continue. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but before Mr. Nikolic addresses you, I would like to make a small correction. When you asked me about the Criminal Code of the Federation, I made a mistake by saying that it was adopted in 1988. My colleagues tell me that this is in the transcript. This was an error on my part. This Criminal Code was enacted in 1998. And this is in line 36:4. The law was enacted in 1998 - to avoid confusion - and this is the law that provides for long-term prison sentences, from 20 to 40 years. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, by this statement, I wish to explain to you in the simplest and shortest way possible the reasons for my guilty plea to Count 5 of the Indictment. I arrived at this decision on my own, without any kind of pressure, threat, or persuasion by my counsel or by the Prosecutors, and I decided to come before this Tribunal and admit that a crime happened in Srebrenica in which I myself participated and for which I expect adequate punishment. I sincerely wish before this Chamber and before the public, especially the Bosniak public, to express my deep and sincere remorse and regret because of the crime that occurred and to apologise to the victims, their families, and the Bosniak people for my participation in this crime. I am aware that I cannot bring back the dead, that I cannot mitigate the pain of the families by my confession, but I wish to contribute to the full truth being established about Srebrenica and the victims there and for the government organs of Republika Srpska, and all the individuals who took part in these crimes should follow in my footsteps and admit to their participation and their guilt, that they should give themselves in and be held responsible for what they have done. By my guilty plea, I wanted to help the Tribunal and the Prosecutors to arrive at the complete and full truth and the victims, their brothers, mothers, and sisters should -- I wanted to avoid their being subjected to additional suffering and not to remind them of this terrible tragedy. Your Honours, I feel that my confession is an important step toward the rebuilding of confidence and coexistence in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and after my guilty plea and sentencing, after I have served my sentence, it is my wish to go back to my native town of Bratunac and to live there with all other peoples in peace and harmony, such as prevailed before the outbreak of the war. Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me this opportunity to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Yes, Judge Argibay, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I wanted to ask you something: You just explained that you are remorseful and you have a great regret because of the crime, et cetera, you want to apologise to the victims. Why did you do it in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, what happened in 1995 is something that I never wanted to happen, either in 1995 or in 1992, when I was expelled because I opposed the extremists. And I hope that you have heard the testimonies of the witnesses who said that because of my viewpoints in 1992, I was physically attacked and mistreated and ended up in hospital for that reason. I did it out of fear that something similar should happen to me again. In 1995, like many other officers who were mobilised, not of their own free will but by a decision of the State, I remained there and I did only what I was ordered to do and what I had to do. I had no possibility to oppose this. And now I regret that at the time all this was happening, I did not again take off my uniform and leave and hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you think that that was what you were to do and you were not able to do that, to just take off your uniform, leave, and hide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tried to do that once. I did not encounter understanding in the place I went to. In the house where I was a refugee, together with my family, it was a flat of 60 square metres and there were 14 of us inside. No one was employed, and I said this in my testimony - this can be checked - I performed physical labour in the Naftagas company. I painted the fence, cut the grass. I did what -- the tasks I was given in order to survive with my family. After this, I went back and, believe me, my family and I in this period did not have any other solution but for us to stay there. I had nowhere to go. I could have gone, but my family, my children, my younger son, who was then four years old, I didn't know where to put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Can you think about the youngest son of all the Muslims Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. killed in the Srebrenica massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, Your Honour. One of the strongest reasons why I have done all this are my pangs of conscience, a pain I have been carrying inside me all this time. And believe me, I owe an apology to all the victims, all the children, all the mothers who have lost their sons, and I especially want to apologise to my pupils.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nikolic, I have one question to you. In your testimony, you told us that you served in a capacity of the chief of the department of the Ministry for Refugees and Displaced Persons in Bratunac and as a coordinator of that ministry for the municipality following your demobilisation in April 1996. In about 15 months that you served in this position, did you take any steps to assist displaced Bosnian Muslims in returning to their homes in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this period there was a law in force on abandoned property. In the period I was working in the Ministry of Refugees and Displaced Persons, the process of the restoration of property was not underway. These laws were adopted later. However, in the Ministry of Refugees and Displaced Persons, by my work there, I contributed in those 17 months to 1.500 decisions on the adaptation and repair of houses and a breakdown of these decisions will show that using ministry funds and the funds of companies from Sarajevo, first of all, the Remontni Zavod, Unioninvest and other companies. I issued a large number of decisions for the adaptation and repair of Muslim houses. All this can be seen and there are documents to show this in the ministry in Bratunac, as well as in Srebrenica, because there was a period of time when I was the coordinator for these two municipalities and I was implementing the then-law and the then-policy in connection with abandoned property. I think by implementing that law, to repair Muslim houses, and using extraordinary funds from these companies, I contributed without paying attention to whether a house was a Serb or a Muslim house to speeding up the return of refugees in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage of the proceedings, are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention to this Bench? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I believe that the hearing is closed, and this Trial Chamber will deliberate on the sentencing issues based on the testimony we heard in this case, as well as the evidence we admitted. The registrar will be instructed for a proper date for the delivering of the judgement, which will certainly be delivered by the winter recess or at the beginning of the next month. The hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.52 p.m.
